h1: Olive Oil Focaccia: Folding the Dough, Dimpling the Top, Pouring at the End
excerpt: Focaccia is not bread you dip afterwards. The oil is folded into the dough itself, pooled again by dimpling, and poured a third time the moment it leaves the oven.
keyTakeaway: Fold oil into a wet dough, let it rise, then press deep dimples across the surface once it is in the tray. Top with rosemary, flaky salt and olives pressed into those dimples, bake hot at 220-230°C, and finish with a last pour straight from the oven.

intro: Focaccia is a wet, olive-oil-heavy dough, not bread you slice and dip afterwards. The oil folds into the dough before the first rise, pools again once the dough is dimpled, and goes on once more straight from the oven — three separate pours, not one saucer beside it.
Get the dough wet enough and the dimples deep enough, and the rest follows.

sections.heading: Why the oil goes into the dough, not onto it

blocks.text: Focaccia dough is far wetter than a sandwich loaf, closer to a thick batter than a ball you can knead by hand. Olive oil goes in with the water, not brushed on after, because a dough this loose needs the fat working through the gluten from the start to keep the crumb open rather than dense.
Two to three tablespoons folded in is normal; more goes on top later. The same oil coats the bowl for the first rise, so the dough pulls away clean rather than tearing when it goes into the tray.

A standard tray needs flour, water, yeast, salt and olive oil in roughly this ratio, with the water kept slack enough to pour rather than knead. Extra virgin olive oil appears three times in the method — folded into the dough, then poured on twice more.

sections.heading: The dimpling step, and the pool it holds

blocks.text: Dimpling means pressing all ten fingertips into the risen dough until they nearly reach the tray, spaced a few centimetres apart across the whole surface. It is not decoration: each dent breaks the surface tension so the dough bakes flat instead of ballooning into one blister, and it opens a well that holds the oil poured over it.

Oiled fingers press hard enough to feel the tray underneath, and the dimples go in right before baking. Oil poured afterward collects in those wells and fries the crust there, while the ridges brown dry — the whole point of dimpling.

sections.heading: Toppings that sit in the dimples

blocks.text: Rosemary, flaky salt and whole or halved olives are the classic toppings, added right after the pre-bake oil pour so they settle into the wells rather than balancing on top, where they would scorch before the crust colours. Rosemary goes on as whole sprigs; salt stays light since the oil already carries flavour.

items: **Rosemary.** Whole sprigs pressed down so the leaves touch the dough.
**Flaky salt.** A light, even scatter after the oil, not folded in.
**Olives.** Whole or halved, pressed into the dimples so they don't roll off.

blocks.text: Focaccia wants a hot oven, around 220-230°C, hot enough that the crust sets and colours before the wet crumb inside dries out. A standard tray takes roughly 20-25 minutes, and it is ready when the top is deep gold and the sides pull slightly from the tray.

items: Mix flour, yeast, water and the folded-in oil to a wet dough; add salt after the first minute.
Cover and rise until doubled, about 1-1.5 hours.
Pour oil into the tray, turn the dough onto it, and stretch gently to the edges.
Rest 20-30 minutes, then dimple firmly with oiled fingers.
Top with rosemary, salt and olives, pressed into the dimples.
Bake at 220-230°C for 20-25 minutes, until deep gold.

sections.heading: The finishing pour, straight from the oven

blocks.text: A last spoon or two of oil goes over the focaccia the moment it leaves the oven, while the crust is still hot enough to drink it in rather than let it sit on top. This pour is separate from the one before baking, and it is what leaves the crust glistening and the crumb underneath soft.

Cut it warm rather than fully cooled. Oil left pooled in the tray is worth mopping up the way you would treat [a saucer of oil beside any other bread](/blog/olive-oil-for-bread-and-dipping) — a dip for the crust, not a dressing.

Oil goes into the dough, into the tray, and over the top: folded in before the rise, poured before dimpling, poured again straight from the oven. The dimples exist to hold that second pour exactly where it lands.

faqs.q: How much olive oil goes into focaccia dough?
faqs.a: About two to three tablespoons folded into the dough for one tray, plus four to five tablespoons split between the tray, the pre-bake pour and the finishing pour after baking.

faqs.q: Why do you dimple focaccia dough?
faqs.a: Dimpling breaks the surface tension so the dough bakes flat instead of ballooning, and it opens wells that hold the topping oil in place rather than letting it run off the tray.

faqs.q: What temperature do you bake focaccia at?
faqs.a: Around 220-230°C, hot enough to set and colour the crust before the wet crumb inside dries out. A standard tray takes roughly 20-25 minutes, ready once the top turns deep gold.

faqs.q: Can I use infused olive oil on focaccia?
faqs.a: Yes, folded in or poured on top after baking. Rosemary and basil, or wild thyme, both suit a rosemary-and-salt focaccia, while the classic oil suits a plainer, olive-only version best.

faqs.q: What toppings work best on focaccia?
faqs.a: Rosemary sprigs, flaky salt and whole or halved olives, pressed into the dimples right after the pre-bake oil pour so they sit partly submerged rather than scorching on the crust.

faqs.q: Why pour oil on focaccia straight from the oven?
faqs.a: The hot crust absorbs it instead of letting it sit on the surface, which leaves the top glistening and keeps the crumb underneath soft. It is a separate pour from the one before baking.
